A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoPL research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original UF-P reward-model experiments for seen and unseen users, GNN accuracy, component ablations and adaptation analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds TL;DR and PersonalLLM results, imbalance tests, further ablations and a 27B-model evaluation.

M1.justification: The proposed signed graph message passing, preference objectives, shared and user-routed LoRA experts, and optimization-free adaptation remain unchanged. Newly tested component removals are ablations; suggested reweighting and active learning are future directions.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only UF-P with discrete preference groups. V2 adds TL;DR summarization preferences and PersonalLLM with continuously mixed user preferences, substantially broadening task and preference coverage. It also evaluates imbalanced user populations.

E2.justification: The benchmark baselines and existing adaptation comparators are retained; Oracle is renamed G-Oracle. Table A4 adds three evaluated message-passing comparator variants removing negative edges and/or activation and feature transformations. The new 27B comparison reuses VPL.

E3.justification: Existing UF-P protocols are retained. Added experiments introduce a 27B Gemma 2 backbone, group-ratio sweeps, 5,000–20,000-user evaluations with an annotation-doubling control, and expert-count sweeps. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, adaptation and pseudo-label analyses, v2 tests majority/minority robustness, user-count and annotation sufficiency, expert-count sensitivity, and the contributions of negative edges, activation and feature transformations. Figures 4 and 7 and Appendix E provide substantial new diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Three-seed reporting and uncertainty values are retained for existing experiments. Appendix E explicitly introduces a single-seed exception for the new 27B evaluation because of hardware limits; Table A3 reports point accuracies without uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original UF-P numerical results are retained, including the 7B results relocated to Table A1. Substantial new results include Gemma-2B seen-user ALL accuracies of 96.58% on TL;DR and 74.85% on PersonalLLM, plus imbalance, sensitivity and graph-ablation findings. Table A3 adds 27B comparisons against VPL.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and equations for propagation, losses, gating and adaptation, including Appendix A, are retained. Added examples, diagrams and discussion of cited theory introduce no new formal assumptions, propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims remain collaborative preference learning under sparse annotations, personalization through MoLE, and optimization-free adaptation to unseen users. The abstract names additional supporting datasets, while the contribution statements and conclusion retain their scientific meaning.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning annotation overlap, uninformative common-pair feedback and majority bias under imbalance. It distinguishes stable preference clusters from declining minority accuracy, interprets the new sensitivity results, and discusses semantic graph construction, active learning and reweighting as possible remedies.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code repository link and construction details for TL;DR and PersonalLLM, including Dirichlet concentration 0.1, response and reward-dimension subsampling, and pair filtering. The existing GNN, MoLE, optimizer, hardware and adaptation specifications are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds recent personalization references, Ju et al.'s message-passing analysis, and sources supporting the new datasets, larger model and imbalance discussion. Its central positioning relative to latent-user models and collaborative filtering remains unchanged; much of Appendix C reproduces the earlier related work.

P1.justification: V2 expands the introductory explanation of sparse supervision, rewrites the dataset narrative, condenses main-text related work while preserving it in Appendix C, and organizes additional experiments in Appendix E. The problem formulation, method exposition and conclusion remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds method and adaptation schematics, a dataset-statistics table, and numerous diagnostic plots and tables. It splits the original combined backbone comparison between Tables 2 and A1 and places a subset of the embedding visualization in the introduction while retaining the full plots in the appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on one benchmark with discrete preference groups by testing summarization and continuously mixed preferences. New imbalance and component analyses strengthen the evidence and expose meaningful failure conditions, which the expanded limitations acknowledge. Method diagrams and the code pointer improve accessibility. The single-seed 27B check and unclear annotation-total wording in Figure 7 limit parts of the added evidence, but the overall empirical support and qualification improve substantially.
